transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-15
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kaur (Redwood SE), Emily Rivera (Willow - Head of ML), Marcus Chen (Willow - Security), Aisha Patel (Willow - Eng Manager)

Summary (auto): align on POC data handling boundaries and benchmark plan; identify success metrics and timeline.

00:00:05 Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intros — i'll run through agenda: scope data handling, logging/retention, prompt storage, and the benchmark plan for the pilot. priya from our se team will go deep on the technicals.
00:00:22 Emily Rivera: thanks jordan, excited. just so you know, our main ask is to ensure no PHI leaves our environment and any PII is redacted or never stored. we want to test with a representative set of clinical notes.
00:00:38 Priya Kaur: yeah totally, and that's common. quick question — will you be willing to provide an anonymized sample or do you need us to run the redaction step?
00:00:46 Emily Rivera: we'll provide an anonymized sample but want to understand what state you're storing prompts and any logs. so if a clinician prompt contains patient name, that should not be persisted in cleartext.
00:01:05 Jordan Lee: absolutely fair. to set expectations: for the hosted POC we have configurable retention and redaction layers. by default shortcode logs are kept for 7 days but we can change that. for Dedicated or Private deployments, you can disable logging and control retention via config — also tie into your KMS.
00:01:28 Marcus Chen: can you explain what "prompts stored" means in practice? are you storing full prompts for quality monitoring? we need that off unless encrypted and auditable.
00:01:38 Priya Kaur: good point. short answer: we store request/response pairs for a limited retention window for debugging and evals, but we offer options: 1) redact PII before storage using our built-in redaction (regex + ML), 2) hash or token-map prompt IDs and persist only metadata, or 3) disable storage entirely. for private deployments you control the storage bucket and KMS keys.
00:02:04 Aisha Patel: and is the redaction on the edge or after the request hits your control plane? i'm worried about data egress.
00:02:12 Priya Kaur: by default in hosted flows we do post-processing in our control plane — there is a short-lived in-memory step; but with Private/VPC we can run the redaction inside your VPC so no plaintext travels to Redwood-managed storage. that's the mode most customers with PHI pick.
00:02:33 Emily Rivera: so for our POC, we probably need either private or dedicated with redaction inside our VPC. we want zero persistent PHI in Redwood logs. is that straightforward?
00:02:43 Jordan Lee: yes, for the POC we can provision a private deployment slice or a dedicated instance and enable local redaction with your KMS. pricing-wise we'll note it's higher but still within pilot scope.
00:02:56 Marcus Chen: talk to me about KMS and HSM. our compliance requires customer-managed keys and HSM-backed key wrapping for production. for POC we could accept KMS with audit logs, but we need to validate integration.
00:03:12 Priya Kaur: we support customer-managed KMS (Cloud KMS) and can integrate with AWS KMS or GCP KMS; HSM-backed keys via your provider are supported for Private. we can show the key rotation logs and give you audit hooks. we'll include the HSM notes in the security doc.
00:03:29 Emily Rivera: great. on retention: what's configurable?
00:03:35 Priya Kaur: retention windows for request logs, debug dumps, and evaluation artifacts are configurable per project. default hosted retention is 7 days; we can set to 0 (no storage) or any custom window. for private you control the storage lifecycle policies.
00:03:51 Aisha Patel: we also want to avoid storing prompts that include PHI even in aggregated embeddings or vector DBs. if you create embeddings from prompts, can they be redacted or not stored?
00:04:03 Jordan Lee: embeddings are an opt-in feature. for the pilot we recommend disabling auto-embedding storage, or if you need embeddings, we can redaction-transform before computing embeddings and store only hashed IDs. we'll include that in the benchmark config.
00:04:18 Marcus Chen: what about telemetry? is there any telemetry that may leak PII, like error dumps containing parts of the prompt?
00:04:27 Priya Kaur: there can be stack traces, but we have sanitizers that run before persistent logs — they scrub common patterns. still, for your POC we'll propose an "air-gap-lite" where debug dumping is disabled and all telemetry is limited to aggregate metrics (token counts, latency histograms) without payloads.
00:04:45 Emily Rivera: sounds promising. now on benchmarks — our success criteria: latency under 250ms p50 for interactive UI, throughput of ~10 requests/sec for async batch, and semantic quality (f1 on extraction tasks) must be within 5% of our current model. timeline: 4-week pilot incl. benchmark.
00:05:06 Priya Kaur: noted. for latency benchmarking we need to know seq length distribution, batching targets, and QPS. can you share sample tokens per request and concurrency targets?
00:05:18 Emily Rivera: typical clinical note is 600-800 tokens, we can sample 5k records for the POC but we'll strip direct identifiers. concurrency for interactive is low (1-2 r/s) but batch jobs hit up to 10 r/s.
00:05:34 Jordan Lee: ok that helps. Priya will draft a benchmark harness that mirrors that distribution. we'll aim to run baseline tests against our curated open model and a quantized variant to compare latency/cost.
00:05:48 Marcus Chen: and what about model fallback and caching — will prompts be cached anywhere? we need to understand KV cache and prefix caching behavior.
00:05:59 Priya Kaur: caching is at the runtime layer for token generation to speed up repeated prefixes; caches are in-memory on GPU instances and not persisted. For private deployments, cache lifecycle is tenant-controlled and cleared on demand. We'll document that caches do not write to persistent storage unless you enable explicit checkpointing.
00:06:18 Aisha Patel: curious about how you handle prompt deduping — we have templates and repeated structured queries and want to make sure dedup doesn't leak variants.
00:06:26 Priya Kaur: deduping is optional; the safe approach is to hash prompt templates and only store hashes + metric aggregates. We'll propose that for your pilot.
00:06:36 Jordan Lee: to summarize technical options: hosted with default retention (not ideal for PHI), hosted + redaction (ok for low-risk), dedicated with customer KMS (better), or private/VPC with redaction in-VPC and full KMS/HSM control (recommended for PHI).
00:06:55 Emily Rivera: agree private/VPC looks right. for the POC we want to validate performance on your runtime — can you commit to a benchmark plan and run it within two weeks of getting our dataset?
00:07:06 Priya Kaur: yes — proposed schedule: week 0 (setup + infra), week 1 (ingest sample data + baseline runs), week 2 (tuned runs and model variants), week 3 (analysis + follow-up). that fits within a 4-week pilot.
00:07:19 Emily Rivera: ok that's doable. question on data deletion: after pilot ends we need proof that all logs and stored prompts are deleted. is there a deletion certificate?
00:07:30 Jordan Lee: we provide deletion confirmations and can export an audit log showing lifecycle events and S3 object deletions for private deployments. we'll also do a retention policy change to 0 and purge buckets. We'll include the deletion checklist in the security doc.
00:07:45 Marcus Chen: one more thing — any chance of model outputs containing hallucinated PHI? we need to ensure outputs don't invent patient identifiers.
00:07:54 Priya Kaur: hallucination is a model behavior; we recommend post-processing checks for PHI (NER-based filters) and confidence thresholds. For sensitive workloads, you can enable output filtering to detect likely PII and redact before presenting to users. We'll include the filter configs.
00:08:12 Emily Rivera: that's critical. we'll want the filter enabled by default for the pilot.
00:08:16 Jordan Lee: noted. we'll turn on output PII filters and include the rule set in docs.
00:08:22 Aisha Patel: circling back to benchmarks — are you supporting continuous batching and token-level cost reporting? we want to see cost per 1k tokens across variants.
00:08:31 Priya Kaur: yes, the Console will show per-request token counts and cost breakdowns by model and quantization. For the benchmark we'll produce a CSV with latency percentiles, throughput, and token costs for each variant.
00:08:43 Emily Rivera: perfect. if we hit the success criteria, we intend to move to a month-long pilot on Dedicated with SLA.
00:08:50 Jordan Lee: great — that would be the natural next step.
00:08:54 Marcus Chen: for the security deliverables we need: SOC2 report, architecture diagram showing data flow, KMS integration steps, and a sample audit log.
00:09:02 Jordan Lee: we'll send those today or tomorrow.
00:09:05 Priya Kaur: i'll attach the benchmark harness and a sample workload config (seq length distribution, batch size, concurrency targets).
00:09:11 Emily Rivera: thank you. any gotchas or blockers we haven't discussed?
00:09:15 Jordan Lee: main risk is dataset anonymization — if you cannot satisfactorily strip PHI we can run redaction in your VPC but that adds time. also HSM integration for production can be more involved but not needed in the pilot if you accept cloud KMS audit logs.
00:09:34 Emily Rivera: we'll try to anonymize; otherwise we'll use in-VPC redaction.
00:09:38 Jordan Lee: cool. let's recap next steps — (1) we send security docs, SOC2, KMS notes; (2) Willow provides sample anonymized dataset and success metrics; (3) Redwood shares benchmark harness + target configs; (4) schedule benchmark run week of 2026-04-27. does that capture it?
00:09:57 Emily Rivera: yes.
00:10:00 Marcus Chen: yes, i'll follow up on HSM requirement details.
00:10:03 Aisha Patel: thanks everyone.
00:10:06 Jordan Lee: thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the benchmark kickoff.
00:10:12 [meeting ends — remainder untranscribed due to recording stop]

Notes on transcription quality: some speaker attributions were fuzzy; short crosstalk and a couple of misheard proper nouns (Willow sometimes transcribed as "Willowh"), but content intact.
